dtz.lead: The final exam of a state-funded integration course — result at level A2 or B1.
dtz.who.title: Who is the DTZ for?
dtz.who.text: The DTZ comes at the end of an integration course and matters to many immigrants in Germany — among other things as proof of German for a permanent residence permit. Depending on the score reached, either level A2 or level B1 is certified.
dtz.fmt.ads.what: Match short adverts to the people they suit
dtz.fmt.tf.what: Understand a newspaper article and judge statements about it
dtz.fmt.forum.what: Match statements to people; understand an interview
dtz.fmt.form.what: Transfer information from an e-mail into a form
dtz.fmt.write.what: A personal reply e-mail + a formal letter
dtz.fmt.speak.what: Describe a picture, then answer personal follow-up questions
dtz.fmt.speak.source: Our own classroom material — 90 sec. describing + 90 sec. follow-up questions
dtz.format.note: The task types above come from our own DTZ classroom material, which also feeds our interactive reading & writing and speaking exercises. According to the BAMF, the written exam takes 100 minutes (listening 25, reading 45, writing 30) and the oral exam about 15 minutes in pairs. Our DTZ model test shows the full structure.
dtz.scoring.title: How the DTZ is scored
dtz.scoring.text: There is no single percentage pass mark. Listening and reading are scored together: 20 listening tasks and 25 reading tasks make 45 points. From 33 points level B1 is certified, from 20 points A2. Writing and speaking are scored separately — each is also reported as A2 or B1. That is why a certificate can read, for example, "listening/reading B1, writing A2".
dtz.set.title: A complete practice set in exam format
dtz.set.text: Nine exam parts, 45 scored tasks — listening parts 1–4 and reading parts 1–5, plus the writing task. At the end comes the evaluation against the official point thresholds, broken down by exam part. Progress stays saved in the browser.

telc.lead: The European Language Certificates — a modular exam system recognised by many employers, authorities and some universities.
telc.who.title: Who is telc for?
telc.who.text: There is a telc exam for almost every CEFR level. They are often required for employment, residence permits and — in the university variants — for admission to a degree course. There are also occupational and specialist versions (telc Deutsch Beruf, Pflege, Medizin); this page deliberately does not cover those — it is about general German.
telc.sprachbausteine.note: Sprachbausteine are telc's speciality: grammar and vocabulary are not asked in isolated sentences but inside a running text. Not every telc exam has all five subtests — telc A1 (Start Deutsch 1) tests listening, reading and writing together and has no Sprachbausteine. From B1 they are part of it.
telc.moreLevels.title: Other levels
telc.moreLevels.text: Above is the telc exam we have a practice test for as a source. Times, task counts and pass marks differ considerably between levels — for A2, B1, B2, C1 or C2 please check the official telc model set for your module. We enter here only what we can document, rather than estimating figures.

goethe.lead: The Goethe-Institut's own exams — recognised worldwide for visas, study and employers.
goethe.who.title: Who is the Goethe-Zertifikat for?
goethe.who.text: Unlike telc, each Goethe-Zertifikat is a standalone exam for exactly one level (e.g. Goethe-Zertifikat B1, not "B1 or B2"). Goethe-Zertifikat A1 ("Start Deutsch 1") is often required for spousal reunification; higher levels are used for study, work and naturalisation.
goethe.modell.title: Model exams for every level
goethe.moreLevels.text: For every level from A1 to C2 there is an official model exam from the Goethe-Institut as a PDF, free and without registration. We took the structure above for A1 from the practice set; for the other levels, times, tasks and pass marks are in the respective model exam. We only enter what we can document, rather than estimating figures.
goethe.a1.title: A1: one exam from Goethe and telc
goethe.a1.text: At A1 there is no separate Goethe certificate and no separate telc certificate: both offer the same exam, Start Deutsch 1 — same parts, same task types, same level. So our practice set works for both. The telc page shows the points and grading scale.

testdaf.lead: Test Deutsch als Fremdsprache — the standard proof of German for university study in Germany.
testdaf.who.title: Who is TestDaF for?
testdaf.who.text: TestDaF is aimed above all at international applicants to universities: the result is the usual proof of German for admission to German universities. Unlike Goethe or telc there is no "level you book" — everyone sits the same exam, and each of the four skills is graded separately with a TestDaF level (TDN 3, 4 or 5).
testdaf.fmt.schreiben.what: One coherent text about a chart or statistic
testdaf.format.note: There is no simple percentage pass mark — each skill is graded separately as TDN 3, 4 or 5, and universities decide for themselves which combination they require. We have no TestDaF source material of our own; the figures here are widely known, public information about the exam format, not invented details. For the exact current times, check the official TestDaF model set.
testdaf.set.title: Practise reading comprehension in exam format
testdaf.set.text: Three reading tasks in the format of the paper-based TestDaF — matching, multiple choice and yes/no/not in the text — plus the writing task about a chart, with structure, set phrases and a checklist. The digital TestDaF is structured differently, but you train the same skills here. All texts and tasks are written by us, not official exam material. Listening is still missing — it needs audio recordings.
testdaf.practice.intro: Besides the practice set above, these three tools are useful across levels and exams — they come from the DTZ classroom material but test general article, grammar and vocabulary knowledge, not TestDaF-specific content.

lid.who.title: Who is the "Leben in Deutschland" test for?
lid.who.badge.noCefr: No CEFR level — a knowledge test
lid.who.text: Unlike telc, Goethe, TestDaF or the DTZ, "Leben in Deutschland" does not test a level of German but knowledge of society, history and the legal order — it is a prerequisite for naturalisation and often closes the orientation course of an integration course.

grammatik.artikel.intro: Every German noun has a gender — and the gender is not in the word itself but in the article in front of it. That is why you never learn „Tisch“, always „der Tisch“.
grammatik.ja-nein-fragen.intro: With no question word, the verb slides right to the front: „Er kommt aus Berlin.“ becomes „Kommt er aus Berlin?“ And a negative question is answered not with ja but with doch.
grammatik.w-fragen.intro: A W-question starts with the question word, and the verb comes right away in position 2. A1: wer, was, wo, wann, wie — and the pattern. A2: wen or wem? welcher or was für ein? mit wem or womit? seit wann, wie lange — and questions in the Perfekt and with modal verbs.
grammatik.praesens.intro: The verb adapts to the person: ich lern-e, du lern-st, er lern-t. The stem stays, only the ending changes — and sein and haben go their own way.
grammatik.verb-position-2.intro: A statement (Aussagesatz) is a main clause (Hauptsatz) that says something. The verb is always in Position 2 — even when the subject is not at the front: „Heute gehe ich ins Kino.“
grammatik.konjugation.intro: Conjugation tables for the most important verbs — present, simple past, present perfect, past perfect and future. To look up and to practise.
grammatik.plural.intro: In the plural the article is always die — but the noun has five ways of becoming more: -e, -er, -(e)n, -s or no ending at all, often with an umlaut.
grammatik.possessivartikel.intro: Whose is it? mein Buch, dein Auto, ihre Tasche. A1: the same endings as ein/eine. A2: in the dative too — mit meinem Bruder, bei meiner Oma, von seinen Eltern.
grammatik.imperativ.intro: Requests, instructions, tips: the imperative puts the verb at the start. A1: Komm! Kommt! Kommen Sie! — with du the pronoun disappears, with Sie it stays. A2: with pronouns (Gib es mir!), reflexive (Setz dich!), together (Gehen wir!) and even more polite as a question (Könnten Sie …?).
grammatik.aduso.intro: These five words join two sentences. They don't change the word order: after them comes a completely normal sentence, and the verb stays in position 2.
grammatik.nomen.intro: A noun is a name: for a person, an animal, a thing, a place or an idea. In German you can spot it at once — it starts with a capital letter and usually has an article in front of it.
grammatik.komposita.intro: In German, nouns are often put together: das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür. The last word decides the article and the plural; the first word says what kind of thing it is.
grammatik.wortarten.intro: Every word has a type. If you know the word class, you know what the word does in the sentence: nouns are written with a capital letter, verbs change with the person — and separable verbs split in the sentence.
grammatik.akkusativ.intro: Nominative → accusative: der → den, die → die, das → das, die (pl.) → die. After haben, brauchen, sehen.
grammatik.dativ.intro: The dative answers the question „wem?“ (to whom?): Ich schenke meiner Mutter Blumen. It follows verbs like helfen, danken and gefallen, and the prepositions aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu. Masculine and neuter take dem, feminine der, plural den — and the noun gets -n.
grammatik.modalverben.intro: müssen, können, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen — they say not what happens but how it is meant: obligation, permission, ability or wish. The second verb moves to the end of the sentence.
grammatik.negation.intro: Two words share the work of negating: „kein“ replaces „ein“ in front of a noun, „nicht“ negates everything else. And „nicht“ almost always sits further right than you expect.
grammatik.perfekt.intro: In conversation, the past is told in the Perfekt. Two questions to settle: which auxiliary verb — and what is the Partizip II?
grammatik.satzstellung.intro: In a German statement the conjugated verb always stands in position 2 — whatever is in position 1. The second part of the verb waits at the end of the sentence: that is the Satzklammer, the sentence bracket.
grammatik.wechselpraepositionen.intro: Nine prepositions can take either dative or accusative. The question decides: „Wo?“ means dative, „Wohin?“ means accusative. Im Kino is not ins Kino.
grammatik.positionsverben.intro: Stellen or stehen? Legen or liegen? The where-to verb takes an object and is regular (Ich stelle die Kiste in den Flur), the where verb takes none and is irregular (Die Kiste steht im Flur). The simple past and perfect of the four pairs come on top.
grammatik.praepositionen.intro: Some verbs need a fixed preposition. Learn the pattern, then practise it in five different task types — like a page from a coursebook.
grammatik.trennbare-verben.intro: With anrufen, aufstehen or einkaufen the verb splits: Ich rufe dich morgen an. The prefix is stressed and goes to the end of the sentence. In the perfect tense, ge goes in the middle: angerufen.
grammatik.zusammengesetzte-verben.intro: With weggehen, losfahren or zurückkommen, the first part already tells you what happens: Der Bus fährt weg. Der Film geht los. Ich komme gleich zurück. It also works without a verb: Der Bus ist weg. Was ist los?
grammatik.als-oder-wenn.intro: In many languages the two are the same word — in German they are not. A single moment in the past is always „als“; anything repeated, conditional or future is „wenn“.
grammatik.n-deklination.intro: A small group of masculine nouns adds -(e)n in every case except the nominative: der Herr, but an Herrn Schneider. Knowing them is what makes a letter come out right.
grammatik.genitiv.intro: The genitive says who something belongs to: das Auto meines Bruders. It also follows wegen, trotz and während. In conversation people often say von + dative — in letters and in the exam, the genitive counts.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination.intro: The adjective's ending depends not on the noun but on what stands in front of it. Three types — definite article, indefinite article, no article — and the pattern is yours.
grammatik.adjektivdeklination-a2.intro: der neue Tisch, ein neuer Tisch: after der/die/das the adjective only has -e or -en. After ein it sometimes steps in with -er or -es. The short version for A2: nominative, accusative, dative – no genitive.
grammatik.ordinalzahlen.intro: First, second, third: this is how you say the date, the floor and the order. Up to 19 you add -te to the number, from 20 on -ste. After am, im and zum it is -ten: am dritten Mai.
grammatik.zahlen.intro: From zero to a thousand: you say the ones first, then the tens, and write it all as one word: einundzwanzig, dreihundertfünfzig.
grammatik.adjektive-nach-sein.intro: After sein, werden and bleiben the adjective has no ending: Die Küche ist klein. Das Wetter wird schön. With nicht, sehr, zu and ganz you can say more.
grammatik.gern.intro: What do you like doing, what not? With gern and nicht gern you say what you enjoy. The word comes after the verb: Ich spiele gern Fußball.
grammatik.praeteritum-sein-haben.intro: War and hatte are the simple past of sein and haben: Wo warst du gestern? Ich hatte keine Zeit. Only with these two verbs do people almost always use the Präteritum instead of the Perfekt in conversation.
grammatik.berufe-mit-in.intro: Der Lehrer, die Lehrerin: for women you add -in, in the plural -innen. With a job you use no ein or eine: Ich bin Lehrerin.
grammatik.konjunktiv2-hoeflich.intro: With hätte, könnte, würde and solltest you sound friendlier: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee. Könnten Sie mir helfen? An deiner Stelle würde ich zum Arzt gehen.
grammatik.infinitiv-mit-zu.intro: An infinitive clause has no subject of its own — the main clause's subject carries over. The „zu“ sits right at the end before the infinitive, and inside the word with separable verbs.
grammatik.praeteritum-plusquamperfekt.in: Three past tenses, three jobs: Perfekt for conversation, Präteritum for narrating and writing — and Plusquamperfekt for everything that happened before that.
grammatik.indirekte-fragen.intro: „Wo ist der Bahnhof?“ sounds curt. „Können Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?“ sounds polite — and turns the question into a subordinate clause with the verb at the end.
grammatik.passiv.intro: Active → passive with a modal verb: subject + modal + … + Partizip II + werden. "Ich buche das Hotel." → "Das Hotel muss gebucht werden."
grammatik.passiv-b1.intro: Die Straße wird repariert – who does it doesn't matter. The passive is formed with werden and the Partizip II: wird gebaut, wurde gebaut, ist gebaut worden. Watch out: in the Perfekt it's worden, not geworden.
grammatik.wortbildung-nomen.intro: Verbs and adjectives become nouns: wohnen → die Wohnung, frei → die Freiheit. The ending tells you the article and often the plural: -chen is always das, -in and -ung are always die.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen-b1.in: Exactly when? Innerhalb einer Woche means: at the latest then. Während des Urlaubs and beim Essen mean: at the same time. Add bis zum Wochenende, zwischen 8 und 9 Uhr and über Nacht.
grammatik.infinitiv-ohne-zu.intro: After some verbs the infinitive stands without zu: Ich kann schwimmen. Ich höre ihn singen. Wir gehen einkaufen. After others you need zu: Ich versuche, früher aufzustehen. Here you learn which verbs belong to which group.
grammatik.funktionen-von-werden.intro: The little verb werden has five jobs: Es wird kalt. Ich werde anrufen. Er wird wohl krank sein. Das Auto wird repariert. Ich würde gern kommen. You can tell the job from what stands with werden.
grammatik.konjunktiv2.intro: With the subjunctive II you talk about wishes and conditions that are not real: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen. You also need it for polite requests and advice: Könnten Sie mir helfen? For the past you use hätte or wäre + past participle.
grammatik.relativpronomen.intro: A relative clause describes a noun more precisely: die Nachbarin, die mir hilft. The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from the noun before it — but its case from its role in the relative clause. The verb goes at the end.
grammatik.irgend.intro: You don't know exactly, or it doesn't matter: just stick „irgend“ in front of a question word, the indefinite article or „welche“ — and the statement is comfortably vague.
grammatik.fokuspartikeln.intro: „Auch ich schenke dir Blumen“ and „Ich schenke dir auch Blumen“ say two different things. Focus particles sit directly in front of the part they highlight — and that changes the meaning.
grammatik.negationswoerter.intro: Beyond nicht and kein there is a whole system: nichts, niemand, nirgendwo, noch nie, nicht mehr — plus the affixes un-, in- and -los, which negate a word from the inside.
grammatik.nomen-verb-verbindungen.intro: „Rücksicht nehmen“, „in Frage kommen“, „zur Verfügung stehen“ — fixed noun-plus-verb pairs in which the verb has almost no meaning of its own left. They have to be learnt whole.
grammatik.partizip-als-adjektiv.intro: A whole sentence becomes one word: „Der Zug fährt ein“ → „der einfahrende Zug“. Partizip I means: happening right now. Partizip II means: finished, or done to it.
grammatik.adjektive-als-nomen.intro: Adjectives become nouns: der Bekannte, die Jugendliche, etwas Neues. They are capitalised and take the ending of an adjective – for people after the article, for things after etwas, nichts, viel, wenig and alles.
grammatik.zweiteilige-konnektoren.intro: These connectors always come in pairs: „nicht nur … sondern auch“, „weder … noch“, „je … desto“. Once you use the first half, you owe the second.
grammatik.konditionalsaetze.intro: With wenn you state the normal condition; falls is more cautious: only in case. Sofern and vorausgesetzt name a requirement, es sei denn the exception. The word also decides where the verb goes.
grammatik.konsekutivsaetze.intro: With sodass and so … dass you state the result in a subordinate clause, with the verb at the end. Folglich and infolgedessen start a new main clause: the verb comes right after them. With a noun you say infolge + genitive.
grammatik.zumal-wohingegen.intro: With zumal you add a second, stronger reason. Wohingegen and während show a contrast, and insofern … als limits a statement. All three send the verb to the end of the clause.
grammatik.modalsaetze.intro: With indem and dadurch, dass you say how or by what means something is achieved. With ohne dass you say what is missing. The verb is always at the end. With ohne and (an)statt the subject decides: same subject → … zu, different subject → dass.
grammatik.reflexive-verben.intro: With reflexive verbs, the pronoun means the same person as the subject: Ich wasche mich. If there is also an accusative object, the pronoun is in the dative: Ich wasche mir die Hände.
grammatik.nebensaetze-weil-dass.intro: After weil, dass and wenn, the conjugated verb goes to the end of the sentence: …, weil ich krank bin. If the sentence starts with the subordinate clause, two verbs stand in the middle: Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.
grammatik.komparativ-superlativ.intro: With the comparative you compare two things: Der Bus ist billiger als das Taxi. With the superlative you say who or what is number one: Das Fahrrad ist am billigsten. If two things are the same, you say so … wie.
grammatik.lokale-praepositionen.intro: Where from? Where to? Where? The question decides: aus der Türkei, nach Berlin, zum Arzt, beim Arzt, nach Hause, zu Hause. You need these little words every day.
grammatik.positionsadverbien.intro: Where is something? Das Büro ist oben. Where are you going? Ich gehe nach oben. Then there are hin and her: Komm her! Geh hin! With these small words you say exactly where something is and where it goes.
grammatik.personalpronomen.intro: Pronouns stand for people and things: ich, du, er, sie … A1: mich, dich, ihn (accusative) and mir, dir, ihm (dative). A2: two pronouns in one sentence — Kannst du es mir geben? —, pronouns after prepositions, and set phrases like Mir ist kalt.
grammatik.indefinitpronomen.intro: For people: man (people in general), jemand (someone), niemand (nobody). For things: etwas (something), nichts (nothing). Ist jemand da? – Nein, niemand. Brauchst du etwas? – Nein, nichts.
grammatik.temporale-praepositionen.intro: When? um 8 Uhr, am Montag, im Mai. With von … bis you give the start and the end. Seit means: it started earlier and is still going on now.
grammatik.futur.intro: With werden + infinitive you talk about the future: Ich werde Sie morgen anrufen. In everyday speech the present tense with a time phrase is often enough. With wohl, the future becomes a guess: Er wird wohl krank sein.
grammatik.temporale-nebensaetze.intro: With bevor, nachdem, während, seit and bis you say when something happens: before, after, at the same time, or up to a point in time. The verb goes to the end. After nachdem the tense changes.
grammatik.da-wo-woerter.intro: For things you say darauf, damit, daran — for people auf ihn, mit ihr. Questions work the same way: worauf? for things, auf wen? for people.
grammatik.lassen.intro: With lassen you say that someone else does something for you: Ich lasse das Auto reparieren. Or that someone is allowed to do something: Die Eltern lassen das Kind spielen. After it comes the infinitive without zu.
grammatik.modalpartikeln.intro: Little words like doch, mal, ja, eben and halt don't change the content, they change the tone: a request sounds friendlier, a question more interested. They are spoken unstressed and sit in the middle of the sentence.
grammatik.adjektive-mit-praepositionen.i: Many adjectives have a fixed preposition: stolz auf, zufrieden mit, abhängig von. The preposition decides the case. After darauf, damit … a dass-clause or a zu-infinitive can follow.
grammatik.konnektoren-grund-gegengrund.i: With weil, da and denn you give a reason, with deshalb the result. Obwohl and trotzdem say: something happens, but not the way you would expect. The word also decides where the verb goes.
grammatik.finalsaetze.intro: With um … zu and damit you say what you do something for. The key question is: who acts in the goal? If it is the same person, um … zu works. If it is a different person, only damit works.
grammatik.zustandspassiv.intro: Die Heizung wird repariert — the technician is still working. Die Heizung ist repariert — the work is done. With werden, the passive describes a process; with sein, a state.
grammatik.relativsaetze-was-wo.intro: Not every relative clause starts with der, die or das. After alles, nichts or das Beste comes was, after places often wo — and wer talks about anyone the statement applies to: Wer zu spät kommt, muss warten.
grammatik.konjunktiv-1.intro: With the subjunctive I you report what other people have said: Die Ministerin sagte, sie habe keine Zeit. You find it mainly in the news and in reports. If the form is the same as the indicative, you use the subjunctive II instead.
grammatik.subjektive-modalverben.intro: Modal verbs don't only say what someone must or wants to do. They also show how sure the speaker is, or where they heard something: Sie muss es gewusst haben. Er soll reich sein. For the past you use the perfect infinitive: gewusst haben, gewesen sein.
grammatik.passiversatz.intro: Das Problem lässt sich lösen. Das Problem ist lösbar. Das Problem ist zu lösen. This is how you say the passive with können or müssen more briefly — typical of newspapers, official letters and science.
grammatik.partizipialattribute.intro: A whole relative clause fits between the article and the noun: der seit Jahren leer stehende Laden. Participle I means active and happening at the same time, participle II means passive or completed, zu + participle I means: this has to be done.
grammatik.nominalisierung.intro: In the nominal style, verbs become nouns and subordinate clauses become prepositional phrases: weil die Preise steigen → wegen der steigenden Preise. This is how reports, applications and academic texts are written. At C1 you need both directions.
grammatik.nominale-praepositionen.intro: Reports, letters from the authorities and specialist texts use prepositions like aufgrund, angesichts or mangels. Almost all of them take the genitive. There are two exceptions you need to know: zufolge comes after the noun and takes the dative, and with dank both are possible.
grammatik.irreale-vergleiche.intro: With als ob, als wenn or als you compare something with a situation that isn't true: Er tut, als wäre er der Chef. The verb is in subjunctive II — at the end after als ob, straight after als.
grammatik.futur-2.intro: The future perfect guesses what has already happened: Er wird den Zug verpasst haben. Or it says what will be finished by a certain time: Bis Freitag werde ich den Bericht geschrieben haben. In conversation people often use the perfect tense instead.
grammatik.es-korrelat.intro: Often „es“ stands in a sentence without meaning anything. Sometimes it only holds position 1, sometimes it announces a dass-clause, sometimes it belongs to the verb for good. If you know when it drops out, you write with more confidence.
grammatik.textkohaerenz.intro: A good text holds together: reference words pick up what is already known, adverbs link sentences, and signposting phrases show the thread. If you use them on purpose, your writing in telc and Goethe C1 is more convincing.
grammatik.verbpraefixe.intro: Die Fähre setzt uns über — sie übersetzt den Text. With durch-, über-, um-, unter-, wieder- and voll-, stress decides: if the prefix is stressed, the verb is separable. If the verb stem is stressed, it stays together.
grammatik.nutzen-benutzen.intro: Many verbs exist with and without a prefix (Präfix): nutzen and benutzen, antworten and beantworten, kommen and bekommen. Sometimes one verb is a part of the other, sometimes they overlap, and sometimes they have nothing to do with each other.
grammatik.verben-als-nomen.intro: You can make a noun out of almost any verb: wandern → das Wandern, die Wanderung, der Wanderer. The ending often already shows the article. And das Wandern is not the same as die Wanderung.
grammatik.artikel-oder-nicht.intro: „Ich würde im Restaurant gerne Fisch essen.“ Why is there no article here? der means: we already know it. ein means: new, one of many. Without an article you speak in general, for example about food, jobs or languages.
grammatik.welcher-dieser.intro: Welchen Mantel nimmst du? – Diesen. welcher (which) and dieser (this) have the endings of der, die, das: welcher, welche, welches – in the accusative welchen, in the dative welchem and welcher. Also: dieser on its own as a pronoun, welcher or was für ein, and jeder.

kultur.duzen-siezen.cardIntro: German has two words for "you": du and Sie.
kultur.pfand.cardIntro: You buy a bottle of water.
kultur.sonntagsruhe.cardIntro: On Sundays the shops in Germany are closed.
kultur.trinkgeld.cardIntro: In a restaurant in Germany you leave a small tip.
kultur.bundeslaender.cardIntro: Germany is a federal state: it consists of sixteen Länder, each with its own government, its own parliament and its own areas of responsibility.
kultur.feiertage.cardIntro: Public holidays in Germany are largely a matter for each individual Land.
kultur.muelltrennung.cardIntro: Waste in Germany is collected separately: paper, packaging, organic waste, residual waste and glass each go into a different container.
kultur.termine.cardIntro: For a great many things in Germany you make an appointment first: at the public office, the doctor, the hairdresser, sometimes even the phone shop.
kultur.anmeldung.cardIntro: Anyone moving into a home in Germany has to register: at the city's Einwohnermeldeamt or Bürgeramt.
kultur.krankenversicherung.cardIntro: Health insurance is compulsory in Germany: since 2009 every person must be insured.
kultur.mieten.cardIntro: Flat listings show several prices side by side, and the biggest of them is rarely the one you transfer each month.
kultur.schulsystem.cardIntro: Education in Germany is a matter for the individual Länder.
kultur.ausbildung.cardIntro: Alongside university, Germany has a second recognised route into a profession: the dual apprenticeship.
kultur.kuendigung.cardIntro: An employment relationship in Germany rarely ends informally.
Germany has public-service broadcasters such as ARD and ZDF (plus many regional and radio stations).
kultur.vereine.cardIntro: A large part of leisure life in Germany is organised — in clubs, the Vereine.
kultur.foederalismus.cardIntro: Ask about "the government" in Germany and you will often get a question back: which one? The federal state distributes responsibilities across three levels, and not by the size of the task but along an order laid down in the Grundgesetz.
kultur.sozialversicherung.cardIntro: Every German payslip lists a series of deductions that together come to far more than the income tax.
kultur.wahlen.cardIntro: The German ballot paper has two columns, and most misunderstandings about German elections begin with the left one looking more important than the right.
kultur.erinnerungskultur.cardIntro: Few areas are as hard for newcomers to place as Germany's handling of the Nazi period, because it is anchored at once in law, in schooling, in the look of its cities and in everyday language.
kultur.grundgesetz.cardIntro: That Germany's constitution is called „Grundgesetz“ and not „Verfassung“ was meant in 1949 as a stopgap — and the name stayed.
kultur.mitbestimmung.cardIntro: Wages in Germany are to a considerable extent set neither by the legislature nor in the individual contract, but negotiated between associations that the state deliberately does not interfere with.

wissen.rights.p2: What deliberately is NOT here: audio and book files from publishers (Hueber, Klett, Cornelsen, telc). We are not allowed to pass those on, not free of charge and not in class either. Official model sets we link instead where they are published — see "Official materials".

vf.about.p1: Quaki kreuzt practises the right-of-way rules from the driving-theory test: rechts vor links (priority to the right), Vorfahrtstraße (priority road), Vorfahrt achten (give way), the Stoppschild (stop sign), the Ampel (traffic light), Zebrastreifen (zebra crossing), turning left with oncoming traffic and vehicles with a blue light. A practice game – not the official exam questions.
vf.about.p2: To read it in peace: the lesson Vorfahrt.
vf.ctl.rvl: No signs: priority to the right
vf.why.blue: Blue light and siren: you must make way at once and wait – whatever the signs say.
vf.why.rot: Red light: you stop at the stop line.
vf.why.stop: At a stop sign you always stop – even if the crossing is clear.
vf.why.zebraPed: At a zebra crossing pedestrians go first. You wait.
vf.why.zebraFree: The zebra crossing is clear: you may drive on.
vf.why.achtenL: Give way (Vorfahrt achten): the car from the left has priority.
vf.why.achtenR: Give way (Vorfahrt achten): the car from the right has priority.
vf.why.achtenLR: Give way (Vorfahrt achten): the cars from the left and the right have priority.
vf.why.achtenFree: Give way (Vorfahrt achten) – but the crossing is clear: you may drive.
vf.why.rvlR: Priority to the right (rechts vor links): the car from the right goes first.
vf.why.rvlL: Priority to the right (rechts vor links): the car comes from the left – it has to let you through.
vf.why.rvlFree: Priority to the right (rechts vor links), but nobody comes from the right: you may drive.
vf.why.leftOnc: You are turning left: oncoming traffic going straight goes first.
vf.why.turnPed: You are turning: pedestrians crossing this road go first.
vf.why.gruen: Green light, and nobody has priority over you: drive on.
vf.why.hsBusy: Priority road (Vorfahrtstraße): you have priority, the others wait. Waiting for no reason confuses traffic.
vf.why.hsFree: Priority road (Vorfahrtstraße): you have priority. Drive on.
vf.why.nxBusy: Priority at the next crossing: you have priority, the others wait. Waiting for no reason confuses traffic.
vf.why.nxFree: Priority at the next crossing: you have priority. Drive on.
vf.heartsTitle: Hearts: a mistake costs one, 8 right in a row win one back
vf.card.hearts: {n} hearts left. {m} right in a row win one back.
vf.card.heartLast: Careful: only one heart left! {n} right in a row win one back.
vf.card.heartsOver: No hearts left – the drive is over.
vf.howBlink: Indicate: when the navi points left or right, set the indicator first – buttons ◀ ▶, swipe sideways · ← →. Straight on and into a roundabout: no indicator.
vf.howHearts: You have 5 hearts. Every mistake costs one, and you see why. 8 right in a row win a heart back.
vf.howLook: Watch the signs, the lights, cars from the right and left, oncoming traffic, pedestrians – and roundabouts, level crossings and narrow spots.
vf.ctl.pfeil: Red light with green arrow sign
vf.ctl.eng208: Narrow spot: oncoming traffic has priority
vf.ctl.eng308: Narrow spot: priority over oncoming traffic
vf.why.gelb: Amber light: red comes next. You stop if you can still brake safely.
vf.why.pfeil: Green arrow sign: stop at the stop line first. Then you may turn right carefully.
vf.why.bahnZug: Level crossing: the red light is flashing, a train is coming. The train always goes first – you wait.
vf.why.bahnFrei: Level crossing: no red light, no train. You may drive over slowly.
vf.why.kreiselBusy: Roundabout: whoever is already on the roundabout has priority. You wait.
vf.why.kreiselFree: Roundabout clear: you drive in – without indicating.
vf.why.eng208Onc: Red sign with a red arrow: oncoming traffic has priority. You wait before the narrow spot.
vf.why.eng208Free: Oncoming traffic has priority here – but nobody is coming. You may drive.
vf.why.eng308Onc: Blue sign with a white arrow: you have priority. Oncoming traffic waits.
vf.why.eng308Free: Blue sign: you have priority over oncoming traffic. Drive on.
vf.why.blinkKreisel: You enter a roundabout without indicating. Only when you leave do you indicate right.
vf.why.blinkMissL: You are turning left: indicate left first – it shows the others where you are going.
vf.why.blinkMissR: You are turning right: indicate right first – it shows the others where you are going.
vf.why.blinkStraight: You are going straight on: no indicator. A wrong indicator confuses the others.
vf.why.blinkWrong: Wrong indicator: you are turning the other way. Indicate the way you are going.

tdf.sourcing: This practice set follows the structure of the paper-based TestDaF: three reading tasks (matching, multiple choice, yes/no/text says nothing) and one writing task with a chart. If you are taking the digital TestDaF, the exam looks different — it has seven reading tasks and two writing tasks (an argument and a summary). You can still practise well here: reading academic texts quickly, checking statements carefully and arguing in a structured way are needed in both formats. All texts and tasks were written by EnglishAcademy — this is not official TestDaF material. Official sample tasks for both formats are free on testdaf.de.

ap.ex.pack.exception: „{word}“ looks like „{rule}“ ({why}) — but takes „{gender}“. An exception.
ap.ex.pack.exception.leicht: „{word}“ does not follow the rule. You say „{gender} {word}“.
ap.ex.male: „{word}“ refers to a male person – words like this are masculine.
ap.ex.female: „{word}“ refers to a female person – words like this are feminine.
ap.ex.kind: „Kind“ is a special case: it refers to boys and girls, but it is grammatically neuter.
ap.ex.kollege: „Kollege“ does end in -e, but it refers to a male person – words for people like this stay masculine.
ap.ex.exception: „{word}“ ends in {ending}, but it is an exception: it is „{gender} {word}“. This word is best learnt together with its article.
ap.ex.in: The ending -in marks the female form (e.g. Ärztin, Kollegin) – words like this are feminine.
ap.ex.chen: Diminutives in -chen or -lein are always neuter.
ap.ex.e: Many two-syllable words ending in -e are feminine (e.g. Tasche, Sonne, Katze).
ap.ex.er: Many words ending in -er – tools, devices and words for male people – are masculine.
ap.ex.el: Many words ending in -el are masculine (e.g. Schlüssel, Apfel).
ap.ex.none: There is no fixed rule for „{word}“ – the article is learnt together with the word.
ap.ex.male.leicht: „{word}“ is a man. Words for men have „der“.
ap.ex.female.leicht: „Frau“ is a woman. Words for women have „die“.
ap.ex.kind.leicht: A child can be a boy. Or a girl. But you always say „das Kind“.
ap.ex.kollege.leicht: „Kollege“ ends in -e. But a Kollege is a man. So you say „der Kollege“.
ap.ex.exception.leicht: The word ends in {ending}. Words like this often have „{ruleGender}“. But not this one. You say „{gender} {word}“.
ap.ex.in.leicht: The word ends in -in. That is the form for a woman. Words like this have „die“.
ap.ex.chen.leicht: The word ends in -chen or -lein. That means: it is something small. Words like this always have „das“.
ap.ex.e.leicht: The word ends in -e. Very many short words in -e have „die“. For example: die Tasche, die Sonne.
ap.ex.er.leicht: The word ends in -er. Very many words in -er have „der“. For example: der Computer.
ap.ex.el.leicht: The word ends in -el. Very many words in -el have „der“. For example: der Schlüssel.
ap.ex.none.leicht: There is no rule for „{word}“. Always learn the word together with „{gender}“.

sprechen.check.a2-bild-nachbarschaftsfes: Separate foreground and background — that is the step from A1 to A2.
A guess with a reason: „Ich denke, das ist …, weil …“

sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.0: „einige … andere …“ is how to describe a group without listing every person one by one.

sprechen.check.a2-bild-wartezimmer.2: A concrete detail from your own life („zwei oder drei Wochen“) is worth more than a general sentence.

One sentence with „meiner Meinung nach“ — giving your opinion is the real B1 part.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.0: „Ich nehme an …, denn …“ joins a guess and a reason in one sentence.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.1: Explain a technical term (Ausbildung, Berufsschule) instead of just naming it.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-werkstatt.2: The why question gets a real answer with „weil“ or „Ein Grund könnte sein, dass …“.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.0: The description shows how you know something („Man erkennt an …“).
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.1: A concrete example from your own life instead of a general complaint.
sprechen.check.b1-bild-buergeramt.2: „Inzwischen …“ shows a development — exactly what an examiner likes to hear at B1.
You respond to the other person instead of working through your list.
Disagree politely at least once — that is what the task tests.
At the end there is a clearly stated agreement on every point.
Konjunktiv II as the polite form: ich würde, wäre, könnten wir.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.0: The description is short. At B2 it is the opener, not the task.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.1: Both pros and cons are there, with the connectors for them: zweifellos, allerdings, dem steht entgegen.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.2: An objection to your own position („nicht nur …, sondern auch …“) shows you have really thought the question through.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wochenmarkt.3: The personal ending is honest rather than model-perfect — that is linguistically harder and sounds more mature.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.0: An observation from the picture carries the argument („Auffällig ist, dass …“) — not just general knowledge.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.1: The objection to your own thesis is included („Man könnte einwenden …“) and answered.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-videokonferenz.2: The difference between „feste Bürotage fürs Team“ and „Pflicht für jeden“ is a nuance. Exactly that separates B2 from B1.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-baustelle-innenst: A detail from the picture (the sign) is turned into an argument instead of just being mentioned.
„weniger …, als vielmehr …“ shifts the question — a strong B2 device.
The statement ends with conditions, not a verdict. That is more nuanced and easier to defend.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.0: A system is explained, not just judged.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.1: Both the counter-argument and the answer to it are there.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.2: „Trennen ist Schadensbegrenzung, keine Lösung“ — a pointed sentence at the end sticks and shows a feel for language.
sprechen.check.b2-bild-wertstoffhof.3: The comparison with your home country does not judge; it describes a difference.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.0: Surname and first name not swapped.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.1: The date in German format: 04.03.1996, not 1996-03-04.
schreiben.check.a1-formular-anmeldung.2: Postcode and town go in separate fields, even if they stand together in the text.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.0: All four points are covered — in the DTZ that is half the grade.
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.1: Greeting and sign-off are there (Liebe Mira / Liebe Grüße).
schreiben.check.a1-nachricht-absage.2: The sentences are short. At A1, „Ich muss arbeiten.“ is better than a long clause with a mistake.
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.0: „Sie“ throughout, including the possessive pronouns (Ihnen, Ihre).
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.1: Requests are questions („Könnten Sie …?“), not commands („Gießen Sie …“).
schreiben.check.a2-email-nachbarn.2: Sehr geehrte Frau Lehmann → Mit freundlichen Grüßen. Greeting and sign-off must match.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.0: The date of birth is spoken, not written: „der zwanzigste November neunzehnhundertachtundachtzig“ → 20.11.1988.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.1: „Neue Patientin / neuer Patient?“ is never said in so many words — you have to infer it from „Nein, ich bin neu in Leipzig“.
schreiben.check.a2-formular-arztpraxis.2: „Das passt.“ means the appointment is confirmed. So fill in both appointment fields.
schreiben.check.b2-beschwerde-reiseveran: Not a word of anger: „muss ich Ihnen leider … anzeigen“ instead of „das war eine Frechheit“. At B2 objectivity is what gets graded, not politeness.
Every defect is set against a promise („Im Katalog … Tatsächlich jedoch …“). A complaint without that comparison is just an opinion.
There is a concrete demand AND a deadline. Without a date no letter of complaint is complete.
Connectors at B2 level: da, ohne dass, andernfalls, daher.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.0: Every field is filled in — in the DTZ an empty field counts as a mistake, even if the information is in the text.
schreiben.check.b1-formular-vhs.2: Nothing made up: what is not in the text stays empty or gets a dash.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.0: All guiding points are covered. One missing point costs more than three grammar mistakes.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.1: Greeting and sign-off match each other and the person.
schreiben.check.b1-brief-david.2: Sentences are linked (deshalb, trotzdem, außerdem), not just strung together.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.0: Read first, then compare — open the solution only once you have marked all the mistakes.
schreiben.check.b1-fehlerjagd.1: Write down your own favourite mistakes. That is the point of the task.

ac.find.final: In “{word}” the last sound got lost. Say the ending so it can be heard.
ac.find.auslaut: In “{word}” the ending sounded soft. At the end of a word it becomes hard: d → t, g → k, b → p.
ac.find.keinE: “{word}” ends in a consonant — don't add an “e”.
ac.find.cluster: In “{word}” consonants come right after each other. No vowel in between.
ac.find.spst: “{word}” begins with sp or st: say “shp” or “sht” — with no vowel before it.
ac.find.verb: In “{word}” the ending was missing. The ending shows who does it: du …st, er …t, ihr …t.
ac.find.ch: “{word}” has a ch. After a, o, u, au it is rough as in “Bach”, otherwise soft as in “ich”.
ac.find.ueoe: “{word}” has ü or ö: tongue as for i or e, lips rounded.
ac.find.h: “{word}” begins with h. Breathe it out audibly — as if breathing on your glasses.
ac.find.rl: In “{word}” listen closely to r and l: l with the tongue up, r at the back of the throat.
ac.find.kurzlang: In “{word}” listen to the length: short before two consonants, long before h or in ie.
ac.find.pb: “{word}” has p or b: p comes with a small puff of air.
ac.find.eiou: In “{word}” listen to the vowel: e is not i, o is not u.
ac.find.hart: In “{word}” the consonant stays hard before e and i — no “y” in between.
ac.find.gh: “{word}” begins with g — not h. The tongue touches at the back.
ac.find.wb: “{word}”: w with the teeth on the lower lip, b with both lips.
ac.find.betonung: “{word}”: stress the first syllable — most German words start strong.
ac.find.s: “{word}” begins with s before a vowel: soft and buzzing, like a bee.

sprachen.title: German around the world
sprachen.lead: Where German is spoken, which languages it is related to – and how close your first language is to German.

sprachen.count.note: Rounded estimate from censuses and official figures.
sprachen.c.DEU: About 84 million people. Besides Standard German there are many dialects – from Low German in the north to Bavarian in the south.
sprachen.c.AUT: About 9 million people. Austrian German has its own words: Paradeiser (tomato), Jänner (January), Sackerl (bag).
sprachen.c.CHE: Four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. About 60% mainly speak German – in everyday life usually Swiss German.
sprachen.c.LIE: A small country between Switzerland and Austria, about 40,000 people. German is the only official language.
sprachen.c.LUX: Three official languages: Luxembourgish, French and German. Most people speak several languages.
sprachen.c.BEL: Three official languages: Dutch, French and German. German is spoken in East Belgium, on the German border – about 80,000 people live there.
sprachen.c.ITA: In South Tyrol German has equal status with Italian. About two thirds of the people there speak German as their first language.
sprachen.c.DNK: In North Schleswig, on the German border, there is a German minority with its own schools and clubs.
sprachen.c.POL: In parts of Silesia, especially around Opole, German is an auxiliary language in some municipalities – on place-name signs, for example.
sprachen.c.CZE: German is recognised as a minority language. Until 1945 millions of German speakers lived here.
sprachen.c.SVK: German is recognised as a minority language – Carpathian Germans have lived here since the Middle Ages.
sprachen.c.HUN: Hungarian Germans are one of the largest minorities in the country, with their own schools and media.
sprachen.c.ROU: Transylvanian Saxons and Banat Swabians have lived here for centuries. German is a recognised minority language.
sprachen.c.NAM: A German colony from 1884 to 1915. Today German is a recognised national language – there is even a German daily newspaper.
sprachen.m.elsass: In France. Traditionally people here speak Alsatian, an Alemannic dialect related to Swiss German. The official language is French.
sprachen.m.pennsylvania: USA. The Amish and many Mennonites have spoken “Deitsch” – a dialect from the Palatinate – for almost 300 years.
sprachen.m.plautdietsch: Mennonites speak Plautdietsch, a form of Low German. Large communities live in Mexico, Bolivia, Paraguay, Belize and Canada.
sprachen.m.brasilien: Many Germans came to Brazil in the 19th century. To this day people speak Hunsrik and Pomeranian here; in Pomerode, German is an official language of the town.
sprachen.m.chile: From 1850 many Germans settled at Lake Llanquihue. There are German schools – and cake is called “kuchen” there even in Spanish.
sprachen.m.russlanddeutsche: Germans have lived in Russia since the 18th century. In 1941 many were deported to Siberia and Kazakhstan; most later moved to Germany.
sprachen.benrath.text: The Benrath line separates Low German from High German. North of it people traditionally said “maken”, south of it “machen”. Simplified on the map.
sprachen.tree.title: The language family
sprachen.tree.lead: German is a Germanic language and belongs to the large Indo-European family. Many languages from Iceland to India share the same roots.
sprachen.tree.otherLead: These languages are not related to German. That doesn't make German harder – it just means you learn words fresh instead of recognising them.
sprachen.tree.names: Language names are given in German – that's what you'll hear in everyday life.
sprachen.cmp.title: How close is your language?
sprachen.cmp.lead: Pick your first language. Eight basic words show how much you already bring with you.
sprachen.cmp.fehler: Typical mistakes with this first language
sprachen.cmp.englisch: English and German are siblings – both West Germanic. Many basic words are almost the same. The word decoder below explains why they still sound different.
sprachen.cmp.persisch: Surprise: Persian is related to German! Both are Indo-European. Compare barādar – Bruder, mādar – Mutter, nām – Name.
sprachen.cmp.russisch: Russian is Slavic – another branch of the same family: брат – Bruder, ночь – Nacht. And you already know cases: Russian has six, German only four.
sprachen.cmp.ukrainisch: Ukrainian is Slavic and distantly related to German: брат – Bruder, ніч – Nacht. Some words even come from German: дах (Dach), шлагбаум (Schlagbaum). And you already know cases – Ukrainian has seven.
sprachen.cmp.polnisch: Polish is Slavic: brat – Bruder, noc – Nacht. Plus many loanwords from German: dach (Dach), ratusz (Rathaus), kartofel (Kartoffel). You already know cases – Polish has seven.
sprachen.cmp.franzoesisch: French is Romance, German is Germanic – both Indo-European. You can still see old roots: nuit – Nacht, trois – drei. And many German words come from French: Restaurant, Büro, Friseur.
sprachen.cmp.italienisch: Italian comes from Latin – and so do many German words: Fenster (finestra), Mauer (muro), Wein (vino), Straße (strada).
sprachen.cmp.spanisch: Spanish is Romance and distantly related to German: noche – Nacht, tres – drei. Hermano, on the other hand, has a completely different root from Bruder.
sprachen.cmp.arabisch: Arabic belongs to the Afro-Asiatic family and is not related to German. But German has many words from Arabic: Zucker (sukkar), Kaffee (qahwa), Ziffer (ṣifr), Alkohol, Algebra.
sprachen.cmp.tuerkisch: Turkish is a Turkic language and not related to German. Still, there are bridges: Joghurt, Kiosk and Döner come from Turkish – and Turkish says otoban (Autobahn) and şalter (Schalter).
sprachen.cmp.chinesisch: Chinese is Sino-Tibetan and not related to German. Good news: German has no tones. And the word Tee came from Chinese via sea trade.
sprachen.cmp.vietnamesisch: Vietnamese is Austroasiatic and not related to German. But you already know the Latin alphabet – that makes reading and writing easier. And German has no tones.
sprachen.cmp.tagalog: Tagalog is Austronesian and not related to German – ina, gabi and bahay have completely different roots. But you already know the Latin alphabet, and you'll recognise many words through English: Haus and house, Wasser and water.
sprachen.cmp.note: Being related helps with vocabulary – for grammar and pronunciation, practice is what counts.
sprachen.dec.title: English → German: the word decoder
sprachen.dec.lead: English and German are siblings: many words are really the same word. German just changed a few sounds – from around the 6th century, the “second sound shift”. That is why water looks almost like Wasser. Know the patterns and you recognise hundreds of words.
sprachen.dec.step1: At the top is a sound swap: the English sound on the left, what it became in German on the right.
sprachen.dec.step2: Below are examples: English word → German word.
sprachen.dec.step3: Try it with a word you know in English: swap the sound – often the German word comes out.
sprachen.dec.note: The first four patterns are the consonant shift, the others later developments. They're rules of thumb – not every word fits.
sprachen.dec.quiz: Try it yourself: what is it in German?

dialekte.title: Dialects in Germany, Austria and Switzerland
dialekte.lead: From “Moin” to “Grüezi”: this map shows the big dialect areas of Germany, Austria, Switzerland and the regions next to them. Click a region for examples, or see how people elsewhere say “Brötchen” and “Tschüss”.
dialekte.map.title: The dialect map
dialekte.map.lead: The colours show three main groups: Low German in the north, Central German in the middle, Upper German in the south. The dots are well-known city dialects and neighbouring languages.
dialekte.map.empty: Click a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.map.wordNote: Simplified: in many places you hear several words, and the Standard German word is understood everywhere.
dialekte.group.nieder.text: In the flat north. The High German consonant shift never happened here: maken, Water, Appel.
dialekte.group.mittel.text: Between the two lines. Some sounds shifted: machen, but often still dat, wat and Appel.
dialekte.group.ober.text: In the south and in the Alps. The most sounds shifted here: machen, Wasser, Apfel.
dialekte.r.nordniedersaechsisch: The “Platt” of the north, from East Frisia to Schleswig-Holstein. Low German is protected as a regional language in Germany. The sounds did not shift here: Water, Appel, maken.
dialekte.r.westfaelisch: Westphalian Platt in the Münsterland, East Westphalia and the Sauerland. Typical is the split s-ch: people say “S-chinken”, not “Schinken”.
dialekte.r.ostfaelisch: Around Hanover, Braunschweig and Magdeburg. Unlike in the north, people say mik and dik for “mich” and “dich”. Today most people in the area speak Standard German, and Hanover is known for especially clear Standard German.
dialekte.r.mecklenburgisch: The Platt of the Baltic coast. In the 19th century, Fritz Reuter wrote whole novels in Mecklenburg Platt.
dialekte.r.brandenburgisch: The old Platt of the Mark has almost disappeared. Today you mostly hear an everyday language in Brandenburg that sounds like Berlin: ick, wat, det, jut.
dialekte.r.niederrheinisch: On the Lower Rhine between Kleve and Düsseldorf. These dialects belong to Low Franconian, just like Dutch. People across the border often understand each other well.
dialekte.r.ripuarisch: Around Cologne, Bonn and Aachen. Typical: g at the start of a word becomes j (jot = gut), and people say dat and wat. The best-known Ripuarian dialect is Kölsch, the language of the Cologne carnival.
dialekte.r.moselfraenkisch: Along the Moselle and the Saar, in the Hunsrück and the Siegerland, as far as Lorraine and East Belgium. Luxembourgish grew out of Moselle Franconian and is now a language of its own.
dialekte.r.pfaelzisch: Palatine, Saarland and Electoral Palatinate dialects belong to Rhine Franconian. In the 18th century, many people from the Palatinate emigrated to America. Their “Pennsylvania Dutch” is still spoken there today.
dialekte.r.hessisch: From Kassel to the Odenwald, with North, Central, East and South Hessian. Known from Frankfurt: ich sounds like isch, and people greet each other with “Ei gude, wie?”.
dialekte.r.thueringisch: In Thuringia and the south of Saxony-Anhalt. As in Saxon, p, t and k become soft: Kloß turns into Gloß.
dialekte.r.obersaechsisch: The “Saxon” of Dresden, Leipzig and Chemnitz, with soft consonants and “nu” for yes. The Saxon chancery language that Luther used is an important root of today’s Standard German.
dialekte.r.ostfraenkisch: The “Franconian” of Nuremberg, Würzburg and Bamberg. Franconia is part of Bavaria, but Franconian is not Bavarian: the r is rolled, and p and b, t and d sound almost the same.
dialekte.r.suedfraenkisch: A small area around Karlsruhe and Heilbronn, between Palatine and Swabian. You can hear a bit of both neighbours.
dialekte.r.schwaebisch: From Stuttgart to Augsburg. Typical: -le instead of -chen (Häusle), isch instead of ist and scht instead of st (Fescht). A well-known saying is “Schaffe, schaffe, Häusle baue” (work, work, build a little house).
dialekte.r.niederalemannisch: In Baden, Alsace and around Lake Constance. The k stays a k (Kind), unlike in Switzerland. In Alsace it is mostly older people who still speak Alsatian.
dialekte.r.hochalemannisch: Most of Swiss German, plus Liechtenstein, Vorarlberg and the southern Black Forest. k becomes ch: Chind, Chuchi. In Switzerland people almost always speak dialect, also on the radio and at work. Standard German is used there mainly for writing.
dialekte.r.hoechstalemannisch: In the Upper Valais and the Bernese Oberland. These dialects have kept very old forms and are hard to understand even for many Swiss. In the Middle Ages the Walser took them as far as Graubünden, Vorarlberg and Italy.
dialekte.r.nordbairisch: In the Upper Palatinate and the Fichtel Mountains. Typical are the “reversed” diphthongs: Bou for Bub, Kou for Kuh, Brejf for Brief.
dialekte.r.mittelbairisch: Bavarian from Munich to Vienna: Bavaria and most of Austria speak the same dialect group. l often becomes i (vui = viel). By the way: the dialect is spelled Bairisch, the federal state Bayern.
dialekte.r.suedbairisch: In the Alps: Tyrol, South Tyrol, Carinthia and parts of Styria. In Tyrol the k sounds like kch. In South Tyrol, German is an official language alongside Italian.
dialekte.m.koeln: Kölsch is the city dialect of Cologne and also the name of its beer. Many carnival songs are sung in Kölsch.
dialekte.m.ruhr: In the Ruhr area, Westphalian, Lower Rhine dialects and the languages of many immigrants mixed into an everyday language of its own.
dialekte.m.hamburg: In Hamburg people split s-t and s-p: they “s-tolpern über'n s-pitzen S-tein”. Moin is said all day long.
dialekte.m.berlin: Berlinerisch is a city language full of wit, the “Berliner Schnauze”. g becomes j: “Ick hab jut jeschlafen.”
dialekte.m.frankfurt: Frankfurt speaks Hessian. It goes with apple wine in a Bembel jug and Handkäs mit Musik.
dialekte.m.wien: Viennese is Central Bavarian with many words from Czech, Hungarian, Yiddish and Italian.
dialekte.m.zuerich: Züritüütsch is the Swiss German of Zurich, which you also hear in many Swiss media.
dialekte.m.bern: Bernese German sounds slower and softer than Zurich German. l often becomes u: viu = viel.
dialekte.m.basel: Basel is an exception in Switzerland: people say Kind with k, not Chind.
dialekte.m.luxemburg: Lëtzebuergesch comes from Moselle Franconian. Since 1984 it has been the national language of Luxembourg, alongside French and German.
dialekte.m.elsass: Alsatian is an Alemannic dialect in France. Many young people there only speak French now.
dialekte.m.friesisch: Frisian is not a German dialect but a separate language, closer to English. It is still spoken in North Frisia and the Saterland and is protected.
dialekte.m.sorbisch: Sorbian is a West Slavic language in Lusatia. Place-name signs there are bilingual, for example Bautzen / Budyšin.
dialekte.lines.title: Two lines divide German
dialekte.lines.lead: In the early Middle Ages, some sounds changed in the south: the High German consonant shift. It never reached the north. Two lines on the map show how far it got.
dialekte.lines.benrath.title: Benrath line: maken | machen
dialekte.lines.benrath.text: North of it people say maken, ik and Water, south of it machen, ich and Wasser. The line runs from Aachen via Düsseldorf-Benrath and Kassel to Frankfurt an der Oder.
dialekte.lines.speyer.title: Speyer line: Appel | Apfel
dialekte.lines.speyer.text: South of it, p also becomes pf: Apfel, Pfund, Kopf. North of it, many dialects still say Appel and Pund.
dialekte.lines.note: English never took part in the sound shift. That is why Low German often sounds almost like English.
dialekte.learn.title: Do I have to learn a dialect?
dialekte.learn.text: No. Standard German is understood everywhere, and you need it for exams, school and work. But it helps to know a few words from your region: Grüß Gott, Moin or Grüezi open many doors. In Switzerland it is worth understanding Swiss German, because everyday life there is almost entirely in dialect.
dialekte.bier.title: The beer map
dialekte.bier.lead: Almost every region has its own beer – and often a story to go with it. The colours show the beer regions, the dots places where a beer style was born or beer history was made. Tap a region or a dot.
dialekte.bier.kind.ober.text: The yeast works at the top, at 15–20 °C. Fruity: Kölsch, Alt, wheat beer.
dialekte.bier.kind.unter.text: The yeast sinks to the bottom, at 4–9 °C, then the beer is stored for a long time. Clear and fresh: Pils, Helles, Märzen.
dialekte.bier.kind.sauer.text: Brewed with lactic acid bacteria, light and tart: Berliner Weiße, Gose.
dialekte.bier.kind.geschichte.text: Places where beer history was made.
dialekte.bier.empty: Tap a region or a dot on the map.
dialekte.bier.r.norden: In the north, Pils is king, often bitter and hoppy. In the Middle Ages the Hanseatic towns turned beer into a trade good: Hamburg and Einbeck shipped it across half of Europe. With Beck's (since 1873), Bremen is still an export beer city today.
dialekte.bier.r.berlin: Berlin has Berliner Weiße: sour, light and served “mit Schuss” (with syrup). In the 19th century it was the city's beer. Today most Berliners drink Pils, but small breweries are bringing the Weiße back.
dialekte.bier.r.koelsch: Around Cologne people drink Kölsch, and only here may it be brewed. In the brewpub it comes in the 0.2-litre Stange, which the Köbes carries around the room in a round tray, the Kranz.
dialekte.bier.r.alt: On the Lower Rhine, from Düsseldorf to Krefeld and Mönchengladbach, Altbier is at home: dark, top-fermented, slightly bitter. Düsseldorf's old town, with its pubs and brewpubs, is also called the “longest bar in the world”.
dialekte.bier.r.westfalen: Westphalia and the Ruhr are Pils and Export country. Dortmund was one of the biggest beer cities in Europe, and big Pils brands such as Warsteiner, Veltins and Krombacher come from the Sauerland and the Siegerland.
dialekte.bier.r.suedwest: In Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland people drink a lot of Pils and Export – but beer is not alone here: in Frankfurt there is cider (“Äppler”), on the Moselle and the Rhine there is wine. Bitburger comes from the Eifel, Karlsberg from Saarland.
dialekte.bier.r.sachsen: In Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt, Pils is the everyday beer. Radeberger near Dresden has brewed in the Pilsner style since 1872, as one of the first breweries in Germany. Leipzig is the city of Gose.
dialekte.bier.r.thueringen: Thuringia is Schwarzbier country: dark but light, with a roasted taste. The best-known one comes from Bad Köstritz. People here say it goes especially well with a Thuringian bratwurst.
dialekte.bier.r.bawue: After Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg has the most breweries in Germany. Export is typical, along with wheat beer and Pils. Near Lake Constance, around Tettnang, a famous aroma hop is grown.
dialekte.bier.r.franken: Franconia, especially Upper Franconia, is considered the region with the highest density of breweries in the world: many villages have their own small brewery. People drink Kellerbier and Landbier, Rauchbier in Bamberg, and in summer they sit in beer cellar gardens under chestnut trees.
dialekte.bier.r.oberpfalz: The Upper Palatinate is the home of Zoigl. Old communal brewhouses still exist here, where the village brews together. A Zoigl calendar shows which home is serving right now.
dialekte.bier.r.altbayern: In Upper and Lower Bavaria and in Bavarian Swabia people drink Helles and wheat beer, strong beer during Lent and Märzen at the Oktoberfest in autumn. The beer garden under chestnut trees exists because brewers planted trees over their cellars to keep the beer cool.
dialekte.bier.r.oesterreich: Austria mostly drinks Märzen, mild and pale, plus Zwickl (unfiltered) and Vienna lager. You order a Krügerl (0.5 l) or a Seidl (0.3 l). Almost every state has its well-known brewery, from Ottakringer in Vienna to Gösser in Styria.
dialekte.bier.r.schweiz: In Switzerland people mostly drink pale lager and order “e Stange” (0.3 l). Until 1991 a beer cartel controlled the market. Since then very many small breweries have opened: today there are more than a thousand.
dialekte.bier.r.suedtirol: In South Tyrol people drink beer as in Tyrol and often speak two languages while doing so. Besides the big Forst brewery in Algund there are many small breweries and brewpubs.
dialekte.bier.r.elsass: Alsace and Lorraine are France's beer region: a large share of French beer is brewed here, and hops grow in Alsace. A small beer is ordered as “un demi” (0.25 l).
dialekte.bier.r.luxemburg: Luxembourg drinks pale lager from its own breweries such as Bofferding and Diekirch. In East Belgium, the German-speaking part of Belgium, Belgian beer culture with its strong abbey and Trappist beers is very close.
dialekte.bier.p.koeln: Kölsch is pale and top-fermented and comes in a slim glass, the Stange (0.2 l). The waiter, called Köbes, keeps putting a new glass in front of you until you place a beer mat on top of yours. Since 1986 the Kölsch Convention has applied: Kölsch may only be brewed in and around Cologne.
dialekte.bier.p.duesseldorf: Altbier is dark and top-fermented. “Alt” (old) doesn't mean the beer is old: it is brewed the old way, as before modern lager. Brewpubs such as Uerige, Füchschen and Schumacher brew their own Alt. Kölsch or Alt? Between Cologne and Düsseldorf that is a serious question.
dialekte.bier.p.dortmund: Dortmunder Export is a strong, pale lager from the 19th century. The name comes from it being sold far beyond Dortmund. For miners and steelworkers in the Ruhr it was the beer after a shift, and Dortmund was long one of the biggest beer cities in Europe.
dialekte.bier.p.jever: In the north people mostly drink Pils, often “friesisch herb”: with lots of hops and clearly bitter. The brewery in Jever has existed since 1848. The big Pils brands from the Sauerland, the Eifel and the Siegerland are also known all over Germany.
dialekte.bier.p.hamburg: In the Middle Ages Hamburg was called the “brewhouse of the Hanseatic League”. In the 14th century it had several hundred breweries, and Hamburg beer went by ship as far as Holland and Scandinavia. Back then, beer was a staple food.
dialekte.bier.p.berlin: Berliner Weiße is a light, sour wheat beer with little alcohol. Most people drink it “mit Schuss”: with red raspberry or green woodruff syrup, from a wide bowl with a straw. Napoleon's soldiers are said to have called it the “Champagne of the North” – there is no proof of that.
dialekte.bier.p.leipzig: Gose is tart and slightly salty and is brewed with coriander. It originally comes from Goslar in the Harz mountains and became Leipzig's favourite beer in the 18th century. In 1966 it was brewed for the last time and disappeared for years; today it is brewed again, in Leipzig and even in the USA.
dialekte.bier.p.einbeck: In the Middle Ages Einbeck was a famous Hanseatic beer town, and its strong beer travelled as far as Munich. There, “Ainpöckisch Bier” slowly became “Bock”. That is why strong beer is still called Bockbier today – and the billy goat (Bock) on many labels is really a pun.
dialekte.bier.p.hannover: In the 16th and 17th centuries Broyhan was one of the most popular beers in northern Germany: pale, light and a little sweet. The brewer Cord Broyhan is said to have brewed it first in Hanover in 1526. Today almost nobody knows it – beer styles can die out too.
dialekte.bier.p.koestritz: Schwarzbier is dark and bottom-fermented and tastes of roasted malt, but it is often lighter than it looks. In Bad Köstritz in Thuringia, brewing is documented since 1543. Goethe is said to have drunk Köstritzer when he was ill and could hardly eat.
dialekte.bier.p.bamberg: Rauchbier tastes of smoke, almost like ham: the malt is dried over a beechwood fire. The best-known smoked beer breweries are Schlenkerla and Spezial. Upper Franconia has well over a hundred breweries and is considered the region with the highest density of breweries in the world. In summer people drink unfiltered Kellerbier in beer cellars under the trees.
dialekte.bier.p.windischeschenbach: Zoigl comes from the Upper Palatinate and is not brewed by a company but in the communal brewhouse that belongs to the whole village. Families let the beer mature in their own cellars and take turns serving it in their living rooms. Whoever has Zoigl right now hangs the Zoigl star, a six-pointed star, outside the door.
dialekte.bier.p.muenchen: Munich is the city of Helles, Dunkel, Märzen and Doppelbock. Spaten brewed the first Helles in 1894, as Bavaria's answer to Pils. Märzen was brewed stronger in March because brewing was not allowed in summer; it became the Oktoberfest beer. Paulaner monks brewed the Doppelbock “Salvator” as “liquid bread” for Lent.
dialekte.bier.p.freising: Beer has been brewed on the Weihenstephan hill in Freising for centuries. The brewery calls itself the “oldest existing brewery in the world” and points to the year 1040; many historians doubt the document behind it. Today you can study brewing at Weihenstephan, and just to the north begins the Hallertau, the largest continuous hop-growing area in the world.
dialekte.bier.p.kelheim: In Bavaria, wheat beer was a privilege for a long time: from 1602 only the duke was allowed to have it brewed. In 1872 Georg Schneider bought this right from the king; the Schneider brewery brews in Kelheim today. Close by, in Weltenburg Abbey on the Danube, beer has been brewed since 1050 – so Weltenburg calls itself the “oldest monastery brewery in the world”. Weihenstephan disagrees.
dialekte.bier.p.ingolstadt: On 23 April 1516 the Bavarian dukes issued a rule in Ingolstadt: beer may only be brewed from barley, hops and water. Yeast was not yet known and was added later. Wheat and rye were to be kept for bread. The word “Reinheitsgebot” (purity law) only appeared in the 20th century, and 23 April is now the Day of German Beer.
dialekte.bier.p.wien: In 1841 Anton Dreher brewed an amber lager in Schwechat near Vienna: Vienna lager. It later became rare in Austria, but the style lives on in Mexico to this day. In Vienna you order a Krügerl (0.5 l), a Seidl (0.3 l) or a Pfiff (0.2 l).
dialekte.bier.p.salzburg: Märzen is the most popular beer in Austria, mild and easy to drink. The Salzburg brewery Stiegl has existed since 1492. At the Augustiner Bräu in Mülln (since 1621) you take a stone mug from the shelf, rinse it at the fountain and have it filled straight from the wooden barrel.
dialekte.bier.p.stgallen: The Plan of St. Gall from around 820 is one of the oldest architectural drawings in Europe – and it shows three brewhouses: one for the monks, one for important guests and one for pilgrims and the poor. In Switzerland today you order “e Stange” (0.3 l), and a Radler is called a Panaché.
dialekte.bier.p.algund: In South Tyrol, German and Italian beer culture meet. The Forst brewery in Algund near Merano has been brewing since 1857. Menus often say both: “Bier vom Fass” and “birra alla spina” (draught beer).
dialekte.bier.p.strassburg: France makes people think of wine, but Alsace is beer country. Around Strasbourg, especially in Schiltigheim, there were many big breweries, and a large share of French beer still comes from Alsace today. Hops are grown here too.
dialekte.bier.p.pilsen: Pils comes from Pilsen (Plzeň) in the Czech Republic. There, in 1842, the Bavarian brewmaster Josef Groll brewed the first pale, clear lager of this kind. It was copied all over the world, and today Pils is the most popular type of beer in Germany.

dialekte.bier.order.lead: Glass sizes and beer mixes have different names in every region.

dialekte.bier.w.kruegerl: 0.5 litres in a glass with a handle
dialekte.bier.w.radler: beer with lemon soda, half and half
dialekte.bier.w.koebes: the waiter in a Cologne brewpub
dialekte.bier.w.deckel: In Cologne, on top of the glass it means: no more for me.
dialekte.bier.w.prost: You say it when clinking glasses – and look each other in the eye.
dialekte.bier.note: Beer is alcohol. In Germany, Austria and Switzerland you can usually buy beer from 16, spirits only from 18. Alcohol-free beer is available everywhere – even as wheat beer.

fs.um.eu.title: EU and EEA: your licence stays valid
fs.um.eu.1: With a valid driving licence from the EU or the EEA you can keep driving in Germany. You don't have to convert it.
fs.um.eu.2: You can exchange it for a German driving licence if you want.
fs.um.eu.3: There are exceptions, for example if it is only a learner's licence or if your licence was taken away in Germany.
fs.um.a11.title: Anlage 11: converting, often without a test
fs.um.a11.1: You can drive with your licence for {f} after you move to Germany. After that you need a German driving licence.
fs.um.a11.2: For every country and every class, the list says: no test, only theory, or only practical.
fs.um.a11.3: You then don't need an eye test, a first aid course or driving school. But the office can ask for a test if it has doubts.
fs.um.ua.1: Since {d}, Ukraine has been in Anlage 11: converting without a test.
fs.um.ua.2: Do you have temporary protection? Then your valid Ukrainian driving licence is valid until {d}, even without converting it.
fs.um.us: For the USA it depends on the state. Look in Anlage 11 and ask the driving licence office (Fahrerlaubnisbehörde).
fs.um.other.title: Other countries: theory and driving test
fs.um.other.1: You can drive with your licence for {f} after you move to Germany. After that, not anymore.
fs.um.other.2: You take the theory test and the practical test. There are no required driving lessons — but a driving school must register you for the test.
fs.um.other.3: You still need an eye test and a first aid course.
fs.um.other.4: The theory test is also available in many other languages. The practical test is in German.
fs.um.other.examples: Examples of countries not in Anlage 11:
fs.um.all.title: For everyone from non-EU countries
fs.um.all.deadline: Apply early, ideally a few months before the deadline ends. If you drive after that without a German licence, you commit a crime.
fs.um.all.extend: Only if you stay in Germany for no longer than one year.
fs.um.all.transl: If your licence is not in German, you often need a translation — for example from the ADAC or from a sworn translator. Ask the office which one it accepts.
fs.um.all.where: At the driving licence office (Fahrerlaubnisbehörde / Führerscheinstelle) where you live. You must go there yourself.
fs.um.all.cost: Depending on the town, about {g}, plus costs for the eye test, first aid course, passport photo and maybe a translation. Ask the driving licence office in your town.

dtzSet.facts.scoring: Scoring: Listening and reading count together for 45 points. From 20 points the certificate says A2, from 33 points B1. The examiners rate writing and speaking against criteria as A2 or B1. A level counts for the overall result if you reach it in speaking and in at least one of the other two parts.
dtzSet.facts.certificate: The DTZ is the final exam of the integration course. With B1 in the DTZ and a passed “Leben in Deutschland” test you get the “Zertifikat Integrationskurs”.
sd1.facts.title: How Start Deutsch 1 is structured
sd1.facts.note: It is the same exam, but the Goethe-Institut and telc count the points differently: Goethe out of 100, telc out of 60. You pass with 60 % at both. At telc the written exam has 10 extra minutes for the answer sheet.

satzmelodie.task1.title: Listen and compare the melody.
satzmelodie.task1.text: Repeat after me: after each sentence you have time to say it out loud. With the microphone 🎤 next to a sentence you can check your own melody – the recording stays on your device.
satzmelodie.caveat: Careful, echo question ↗↗: „Du kommst morgen?“ is not a normal question. In a yes/no question the verb comes first: „Kommst du morgen?“ The echo question keeps the word order of a statement; only the voice goes up sharply. It also means something different: you're surprised or checking that you heard right („Wirklich? Du kommst morgen?“). In writing and in exams: verb in position 1.

satzmelodie.rule.title: The melody at the end of the sentence
satzmelodie.rule.aussage: The voice falls at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.w: The voice falls at the end. To sound friendly: slightly up at the end.
satzmelodie.rule.jn: The verb is in position 1. The voice rises.
satzmelodie.rule.echo: Word order like a statement, the voice rises sharply. Not a normal question: you're surprised or checking. The yes/no question has the verb in position 1 („Kommen Sie aus Polen?“).
satzmelodie.rule.ausruf: The stressed word goes way up, then the voice falls sharply. Feeling: joy, anger, surprise.
satzmelodie.rule.liste: The voice stays up → until the list is finished. Then it falls ↘.
