wissen.lernen.lead: Mistakes are allowed. Even more: without mistakes you learn more slowly. Here Bruno, Regi, Hamsti and Quaki explain how your brain really holds on to German.
wissen.lernen.jungle.title: Your brain is a jungle
wissen.lernen.jungle.lead: Imagine this: a new word lies on the other side of a dense jungle. There's no path to it yet. You have to cut it yourself.
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.title: The machete
wissen.lernen.jungle.machete.text: Learning is your machete. On your first try you hack your way through the jungle with effort. That's tiring – and completely normal.
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.title: The wrong way
wissen.lernen.jungle.falsch.text: Sometimes you walk in the wrong direction: a mistake. Your brain notices the difference between what it expected and the right answer. That very signal shows it where the path really goes.
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.title: The beaten path
wissen.lernen.jungle.pfad.text: Every time you walk the path again, it gets wider. Nerve cells that often work together connect more strongly.
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.title: The road
wissen.lernen.jungle.strasse.text: After many repetitions the path has become a road. You don't have to think anymore – the word is just there. Practice even changes the wiring in your brain along the way.
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot1: And a path you don't walk for a long time? It slowly grows over again. That's why you repeat (Rule 3).
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot2: Your brain constantly rebuilding itself like this is called neuroplasticity. Adults who learn to juggle for three months have measurably more grey matter afterwards
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot4: And London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus
wissen.lernen.jungle.foot5: Your brain learns at any age.
wissen.lernen.wheel.label: The seven rules
wissen.lernen.wheel.title: The learning circle
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.title: Making mistakes is part of it
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.text: You're not supposed to get everything right straight away. If you try an answer, get it wrong and then see the right one, you remember it better than if you only read it.
wissen.lernen.rule.fehler.why: A mistake surprises your brain. That surprise makes the correction stick. Even mistakes you were completely sure about get corrected especially well afterwards. The only important thing: always look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.say: Hmm … what was it called again?
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.title: Recall first, then check
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.text: Reading a word list five times feels good – but doesn't do much. Better: cover the word and quiz yourself. Only then do you check.
wissen.lernen.rule.erinnern.why: Every time you pull a word out of your head, the path to it gets wider. Reading only goes through your eyes. Remembering is work, and that very work is what stays.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.title: A little, but often – and sleep well
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.text: Ten minutes every day are better than two hours on Sunday. And when you've almost forgotten a word, that's the best moment to review it.
wissen.lernen.rule.oft.why: With breaks between reviews, knowledge stays much longer. While you sleep, your brain sorts what you learned during the day. So learning in the evening and a quick review in the morning go well together.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.title: Mix instead of blocks
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.text: Twenty sentences with only the accusative are easy – you already know what's coming. In real life you don't. So mix it up: accusative, dative, perfect tense, all jumbled.
wissen.lernen.rule.mischen.why: When you mix, you learn not only the rule but also when you need it. That's harder, but it's exactly what you need in conversation and in the exam.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.title: Speak out loud, don't just read
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.text: Read new sentences out loud. Speak along when you listen to audio. Even alone in the kitchen – that's not weird, that's training.
wissen.lernen.rule.laut.why: What you say out loud, you also hear, and you move your mouth while doing it. So your head remembers the sentence in several ways. And your mouth learns the words before you need them in a conversation.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.title: It can be hard – but not too hard
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.text: If everything is easy, you learn little. If everything is too hard, you give up. You learn the most in between: you have to think, but you usually manage.
wissen.lernen.rule.schwer.why: The effort isn't a sign that you're bad at it. It's the sign that you're learning right now. Choose your level so that you get about eight out of ten tasks right.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.title: Celebrate small steps
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.text: Don't compare yourself with others. Compare yourself with yourself a month ago. Every new word is a step.
wissen.lernen.rule.feiern.why: Anyone who sees their progress keeps learning. Small goals that you really reach keep you going longer than one big goal that's far away.
wissen.lernen.sum.title: In short
wissen.lernen.sum.1: Try it yourself first – even if you get it wrong.
wissen.lernen.sum.2: After every mistake, look at the right answer.
wissen.lernen.sum.3: Better a little every day than a lot once.
wissen.lernen.sum.4: Mix the topics and speak out loud.
wissen.lernen.studies.title: The studies
wissen.lernen.studies.lead: The asterisks (*) in the text lead here. The studies are in English.
wissen.lernen.study.schultz: The brain signals the difference between expectation and outcome – this error signal steers learning.
wissen.lernen.study.rumelhart: Artificial neural networks learn by correcting their connections a little after every error.
wissen.lernen.study.hebb: Nerve cells that are often active at the same time connect more strongly – the basic idea behind the „Trampelpfad“ (beaten path).
wissen.lernen.study.bengtsson: A lot of practice changes the nerve pathways themselves (the white matter).
wissen.lernen.study.draganski: After three months of juggling, adults' grey matter grew – and shrank back when they stopped.
wissen.lernen.study.boyke: The same works for people around 60, too.
wissen.lernen.study.maguire: London taxi drivers, who learn thousands of streets, have a changed hippocampus – the longer in the job, the clearer it is.
wissen.lernen.study.kornell: Guessing wrong first and then seeing the answer helps more than reading the answer straight away.
wissen.lernen.study.butterfield: Mistakes you were sure about are remembered especially well after they are corrected.
wissen.lernen.study.metcalfe: Overview: mistakes that get corrected help learning instead of harming it.
wissen.lernen.study.roediger: Quizzing yourself keeps knowledge longer than reading it again.
wissen.lernen.study.cepeda: Reviewing with breaks in between beats learning in one go.
wissen.lernen.study.rasch: During sleep the brain consolidates what was learned during the day.
wissen.lernen.study.rohrer: Mixed tasks did clearly better in the later test than tasks in blocks.
wissen.lernen.study.macleod: Words read aloud are remembered better than words read silently.
wissen.lernen.study.bjork: „Wünschenswerte Schwierigkeiten“ (desirable difficulties): what feels hard while practising often stays longer.
wissen.lernen.study.wilson: Learning models make the fastest progress when they get about 85% of the tasks right.

wortfallen.lead: Some words sound almost the same – and mean something completely different. Here are the {n} funniest traps, each with a memory trick.
wortfallen.kueche.m3: the man who cooks (die Köchin: the woman)
wortfallen.kueche.react: A whole kitchen? With stove and sink? You must be strong!
wortfallen.kueche.tip: One sentence for all three: Der Koch backt in der Küche einen Kuchen.
wortfallen.schenken.m2: to send by post or by email
wortfallen.schenken.m3: meat from a pig, e.g. on bread
wortfallen.schenken.react: A book with ham? Well … maybe in Bavaria.
wortfallen.schenken.tip: schenken → das Geschenk: both with „e“. schicken → with „i“ as in Brief. And the Schinken is what you eat.
wortfallen.kirche.m1: where Christians pray, with a tower and a bell
wortfallen.kirche.react: With a tower and a bell? Enjoy your meal!
wortfallen.kirche.tip: Kirsche has one „s“ more – „s“ as in süß (sweet).
wortfallen.schluessel.m1: you open the door with it
wortfallen.schluessel.m2: deep plate for soup or muesli
wortfallen.schluessel.react: Then you'll need a very small spoon.
wortfallen.schluessel.tip: The „l“ in Schlüssel fits into the lock: Schlüssel – Schloss.
wortfallen.kissen.m1: your head lies on it in bed
wortfallen.kissen.react: You want to sleep on me? That's … weird.
wortfallen.kissen.tip: küssen → der Kuss: always with „u“ or „ü“. The Kissen lies on the bed.
wortfallen.bett.m2: patch of garden with flowers or vegetables
wortfallen.bett.tip: Bett: short „e“, two „t“. Beet: long „e“, two „e“ – flowers grow there.
wortfallen.zahlen.tip: Die Kinder zählen, die Eltern zahlen. With „ä“ you count, without „ä“ you pay.
wortfallen.gift.m1: makes you ill or kills (English: poison)
wortfallen.gift.m2: you get it on your birthday (English: gift)
wortfallen.gift.react: Oh … thanks. I'll open it later. Maybe.
wortfallen.gift.tip: A „falscher Freund“ (false friend) from English: in German, Gift is never a present.
wortfallen.bekommen.m2: to change, to be something later (English: become)
wortfallen.bekommen.react: Do you want to order one? With delivery?
wortfallen.bekommen.tip: Another false friend: „become“ means werden. Bekommen is „get“.
wortfallen.schoen.tip: The two dots on the „ö“ are eyes – they see something beautiful.
wortfallen.liegen.m1: to be lying flat in bed or on the sofa
wortfallen.liegen.react: And who are you telling stories to there?
wortfallen.liegen.tip: lügen → die Lüge: both with „ü“. Liegen with „ie“ as in Liegestuhl (deck chair).
wortfallen.wahl.m1: people vote, e.g. for the government
wortfallen.wahl.m2: the biggest animal in the sea
wortfallen.wahl.tip: Wahl comes from wählen – that's why it has the „h“. The Wal swims without one.
wortfallen.huette.m1: small house, often in the mountains
wortfallen.huette.react: So how many people fit in your hat?
wortfallen.huette.tip: Hütte: short „ü“, two „t“. Hüte: long „ü“ – lots of hats on lots of heads.
wortfallen.bier.react: The waiter is a bit scared now.
wortfallen.bier.tip: Bier with „ie“ as in „vier Bier“. Bär with „ä“. Beere with two „e“.
wortfallen.maedchen.react: And what does the girl say about that?
wortfallen.maedchen.tip: Märchen with „r“ as in Rotkäppchen (Little Red Riding Hood).
wortfallen.fuehlen.tip: fühlen with „h“ as in das Gefühl (feeling). füllen with „ll“ like a full glass.
wortfallen.hoehle.react: At least it's nice and warm there.
wortfallen.hoehle.tip: Höhle: long „ö“ with „h“. Hölle: short „ö“ with „ll“ – hot!
wortfallen.schwuel.react: The weather loves whoever it wants. But what you meant was: hot and humid.
wortfallen.schwuel.tip: The two dots on the „ü“ are drops of sweat: schwül.

verben.title: The most important verbs
verben.mascot: You need these verbs every day.
verben.lead: A mini grammar to look things up: {n} verbs, each in Präsens, Präteritum and Perfekt. Whatever doesn't follow the pattern is <mark class="vb-x">highlighted</mark> — that's what you have to learn.
verben.group.hilfsverb.name: Auxiliary verbs
verben.group.hilfsverb.what: You need them for the Perfekt, passive and future – and they're irregular in every tense.
verben.group.modal.name: Modal verbs
verben.group.modal.what: They say whether you can, must, may or want to do something – almost always together with a second verb.
verben.group.unregelmaessig.name: Irregular verbs
verben.group.unregelmaessig.what: A new vowel in the Präteritum, participle often ending in -en. Often also a vowel change with du and er.
verben.group.regelmaessig.name: Regular verbs
verben.group.regelmaessig.what: Stem + ending, Präteritum with -te, participle ge- … -t. That's how almost all verbs work.
verben.group.trennbar.name: Separable verbs
verben.group.trennbar.what: The prefix goes to the end of the sentence: Ich stehe um sieben auf. In the participle, ge sits in the middle.

hs.about.title: What is this about?
hs.about.p: Hamstis Wachtelhuhn practises listening comprehension and vocabulary at the same time: you hear each word with its article, just as it is spoken in class, and have to recognise it quickly. Reloading brings article and picture questions. All words come from our vocabulary – you can also practise them there at your own pace.

kt.t.title: Placement test for your class
kt.t.lead: Your class takes the test on their phones via a QR code, with their names and without an account. You see each person's level, from A1 to B2, and which topics they haven't got yet. Or run a topic test to check the grammar of one level. The questions come from our grammar exercises; you can edit any of them.
kt.t.signin.title: Sign in to create a test
kt.t.signin.text: The results belong to your account, so you can still see them next week. The account is free. Your students don't need one.
kt.t.teacher.text: Then turn on the teacher tools: class tests, surveys, classes and your own live quizzes. You can turn them off again at any time under Settings in your account.

kt.t.art.einstufungInfo: Where is each person? Questions across several levels, from easy to hard. You see each person's level.
kt.t.art.themaInfo: Has the class got the grammar of one level? You choose the topics and see which ones need more work.
kt.t.umfang.kurzInfo: About 10 to 15 minutes. Good for the first day of a course.
kt.t.umfang.langInfo: About an hour for A1 to B2, less with fewer levels. One reading text and one listening text per level, plus a writing task that you mark. Everyone needs headphones for the listening.
kt.t.preview.hint: This is what the test looks like, with the correct answer first. You can edit any question and its answers or write your own; they stay when you reshuffle. Each phone shows the answers in a different order.
kt.t.how.title: How the test works
kt.t.how.1: The class scans the QR code, enters their names and answers one question after another. They can skip questions.
kt.t.how.2: Each phone can submit once. Afterwards each person sees their own score and which questions were wrong, but not the answers. You go through those with the class.
kt.t.how.3: We save the name, the answers and the score. No account, no email, no IP address. You can delete single results or the whole test.
